analysis.one_liner: Fast-tracks oil, gas, and pipeline permits, curbs environmental review, and ends the electric-vehicle tax credit early.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, it sat there with zero cosponsors until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force federal agencies and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve or deny energy permits within 60 days, exempt oil and gas pipelines and power lines from presidential permits, and let states take over oil and gas permitting on federal land. It would also wipe out a Biden-era climate executive order, write two 2020 Trump-era environmental rules into law, and end the electric-vehicle tax credit after 2024 instead of 2032. The practical effect is faster approval of fossil fuel projects with less environmental review, and a higher effective price for electric cars.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, oil and gas producers, pipeline builders, and LNG terminal developers would have gained the most: 60-day approval deadlines, no presidential permit for cross-border pipelines, state control of permitting on federal land, and permanently weaker environmental review rules. Solar, wind, and geothermal projects would also get the fast-track deadlines. Electric-car buyers would lose out, since the up-to-$7,500 clean vehicle credit would expire at the end of 2024.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, pipeline, and LNG developers

how_it_helps.text: It would require federal agencies to approve or deny every pending and future permit for natural gas, oil and gas leasing and drilling, pipelines, LNG terminals, and renewable energy projects within 60 days, with only a 30-day extension possible.

It would remove the presidential permit requirement for cross-border oil and natural gas pipelines and electric transmission lines, a power presidents have used to block or delay projects like Keystone XL.
It would let states, on request, take over the federal permitting process for oil and gas development on federal land inside their borders.

It would rescind Executive Order 13990, the Biden administration's order directing agencies to address climate change and protect public health and the environment, and permanently enact the 2020 Trump-era rules that shortened National Environmental Policy Act reviews and narrowed which waters are federally protected.
It would terminate the clean vehicle tax credit for cars placed in service after 2024, eight years earlier than current law, reducing federal spending on EV subsidies.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of electric vehicles would pay up to thousands more per car once the credit ended. Communities near pipelines, LNG terminals, and drilling would get less say and weaker environmental review before construction. Waterways and wetlands no longer covered by the codified 2020 rule would lose federal protection. And because federal land belongs to all Americans, shifting its permitting decisions to individual states would reduce public oversight of how it is developed.
analysis.who_pays_short: EV buyers and communities near energy projects

drawbacks.text: Ending the clean vehicle credit after 2024 instead of 2032 would raise the effective price of an electric car by as much as $7,500 for buyers, just as the market was expanding.

A 60-day deadline for FERC decisions, extendable only by an act of Congress, would push the commission to approve complex pipeline and LNG projects it has not fully reviewed, since a denial would require a detailed written justification to Congress within five days.
Writing the 2020 Navigable Waters Protection Rule into law would strip federal protection from many streams and wetlands, affecting drinking water sources and flood control, not just industry costs.

Delegating oil and gas permitting on federal land to the states would let the government next door decide how land owned by all Americans is developed, with the permitting agency's interests aligned with local industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster permitting addresses a real problem — energy projects of all kinds sit in review for years — and the bill's deadlines cover renewable projects too. But the bill buys speed by weakening review rather than funding faster agencies, bundles in provisions that go well beyond speed (rescinding the climate order, entrenching the narrower water rule, ending the EV credit, shifting federal land decisions to states), and the scale of the giveaway to fossil fuel developers outweighs the genuine permitting reform. It was also structurally unrealistic: the zero-cosponsor sponsor list and the demand that FERC extensions pass both chambers as standalone laws signaled it was a statement bill, not a workable one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended, killing it.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott introduced the bill on March 14, 2023, with no cosponsors from either party.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers kept the electric-vehicle tax credit through 2032, and the existing environmental review and water-protection rules stayed in place. Oil, gas, pipeline, and LNG developers did not get the fast-track approvals, state takeover of federal land permitting, or exemption from presidential permits they would have gained.

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and the only member to put his name on it.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the record shows no committee action after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only its Republican sponsor supported it — zero cosponsors from either party — and it never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would hand them 60-day permit deadlines, state control of permitting on federal land, permanently weaker environmental review, and rescission of the federal climate order. The gains come from reduced review and reduced public oversight of development on federally owned land.

Cross-border pipelines and LNG projects would skip presidential permits entirely, and FERC would have to approve or deny their applications in 60 days with extensions requiring an act of Congress — pressure that favors approval.
Terminating the clean vehicle credit after 2024 instead of 2032 removes a subsidy that supported EV demand; the industry's loss here runs alongside the loss to car buyers.

Solar, wind, geothermal, and storage projects would get the same 60-day permitting deadlines, a genuine benefit; but rescinding the climate executive order and ending the EV credit would undercut the demand and policy environment they depend on.

The bill would exempt electric transmission facilities, including cross-border lines, from presidential permit requirements and speed approvals, easing grid buildout that the public also wants — though bundled in a bill whose main thrust serves fossil fuels.
